items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
Two friends on a beach try to get **drinking water** from sea water: one leaves it in the sun, one catches the steam on a cold lid.

Salt water in a dish and copper sulphate crystals show **evaporation** and **crystallisation**; the set-up for **distillation** gets the liquid back. A black ink spot introduces **paper chromatography**. Oil and water, camphor and sand, and a spinning blood sample show the **separating funnel**, **sublimation** and **centrifugation**. A flow chart helps students **choose** a method.

Some pictures have a **second picture or animation**: show picture 1, ask, then click ›.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures; solutions, colloids and suspensions

• saturated solutions; crystals separate out when a hot saturated solution cools

• boiling, evaporation and condensation; filtration

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Explain evaporation, crystallisation and distillation with labelled diagrams.

**2.** Explain chromatography, sublimation, separating funnel and centrifugation.

**3.** Choose the right separation method for a given mixture.

chunks.name: Pure crystals from an impure solid

items.text:
**Step 1: picture 1 of 4**

(a) Impure copper sulphate is stirred into hot water until no more dissolves: a **hot saturated solution**. The brown specks are dust. **Do not click › yet.**

**Step 2: click › (now 2 of 4)**

(b) The hot solution is poured through filter paper. Ask Question 4 before clicking again.

**Answer to Question 4**

**Step 3.** Take guesses first. To remove **insoluble impurities** such as dust. The copper sulphate is dissolved, so it passes through the filter paper. Now click › (pointer 4).

**Step 4: click › (now 3 of 4)**

After Question 4. The dust is caught on the filter paper; (c) the clear filtrate is left to cool slowly and crystals form.

**Answer to Question 5**

**Step 5.** Take guesses first. **Still dissolved** in the leftover liquid. There is too little of it to saturate the solution, so it does not crystallise. Now click › (pointer 6).

**Step 6: click › (now 4 of 4)**

After Question 5. A zoomed-in view of the cooling filtrate: copper sulphate particles join the crystals; the orange impurity particles stay dissolved.

*Picture 4 is animated: it plays on its own and repeats. Click **‹** to return to picture 3 and stop it.*

**Step 7**

Read the key idea: **crystallisation**.

items.prompt: True or false? Evaporation and crystallisation are the same process.
options: True: both need heating to dryness

items.prompt: The best way to get sugar from a sugar solution is

items.text:
**On this question**

**B**: false. Evaporation leaves behind everything that was dissolved; crystallisation gives pure crystals and leaves the impurities in the liquid.

**On this question**

**B**: sugar burns when heated to dryness; crystallisation gives pure sugar crystals.

items.prompt: Alcohol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C. Can simple distillation separate them?

items.text:
**On this question**

**C**: their boiling points are only **22 °C** apart, less than 25 °C, so **fractional distillation** is used.

items.prompt: Is sublimation the same as evaporation?
options: No: sublimation starts from a solid
No: evaporation starts from a gas

items.prompt: Cream is separated from milk by

items.text:
**On this question**

**B**: in sublimation a **solid** turns directly into vapour; in evaporation a **liquid** turns into vapour.

**On this question**

**C**: the milk is spun fast and the lighter cream collects separately from the rest.
